article: Disco's story is often told starting with Saturday Night Fever, but the real history starts five years earlier and in a very different room. From around 1970, DJs in New York clubs serving Black, Latino and gay audiences — spaces largely excluded from the era's mainstream nightlife — built a continuous, beat-matched dance culture around soul, funk and early electronic production. Donna Summer and producer Giorgio Moroder's 1977 "I Feel Love" pushed the genre toward the synthesizer-heavy sound that would define its late period, around the same time Saturday Night Fever carried a polished, largely white version of disco culture to a mass audience and, with it, the mirror ball and metallic lamé look most people now picture. That mainstream wave didn't last: a backlash culminated in 1979's "Disco Demolition Night," a Chicago baseball-stadium event where a crate of disco records was blown up between games, an incident historians have since read as carrying real hostility toward the genre's Black and gay roots. Disco's visual language — mirror balls, metallic fabric, saturated stage lighting — nonetheless outlived the backlash, feeding directly into 1980s glam and, decades later, into revival aesthetics like eighties-neon.
